title: Aghorebhyo ’tha ghorebhyaḥ: the third of the five ‘brahma’ mantras
theme: Homage to all the forms of Rudra — the gentle, the terrible and the most terrible: the southern face, by the commentators’ account.

words.context: The anonymous commentator: «विग्रहा अघोराः सात्विकत्वेन शान्ताः सौम्याः» — forms calm and gentle, being sattvic
The anonymous commentator: «अन्ये तु घोरा राजसत्वेनोग्राः» — fierce, being rājasic

words.meaning: to those more terrible than the terrible
words.context: The anonymous commentator: «अपरे तु तामसत्वेन घोरादपि» — still more terrible, being tāmasic

words.base: सर्व (as printed; शर्व in the commentators’ texts)
शर्व (as printed; सर्व in the commentators’ texts)

sandhi.rule: aghorebhyaḥ + atha → aghorebhyo ’tha: -aḥ becomes -o and the following a is elided (P. 6.1.109 (एङः पदान्तादति)).
sarvebhyaḥ + sarva → sarvebhyas sarva (P. 8.3.36 (वा शरि)); the recitation writes the double sibilant.

sandhi_exceptions.note: te · astu: classical te ’stu; every witness, and Sāyaṇa’s text, keeps the vowels apart.

morphology.note: ghoratara is the comparative of ghora; prefixed by ghora it means ‘more terrible than the terrible’. Bhāskara: «घोरेभ्योपि घोरतरेभ्यस् त्वत्तोपि घोरतरेभ्यः».

As printed the line reads sarvebhyas sarva śarvebhyo. The texts of Sāyaṇa and the Tirupati e-text read sarvataḥ śarva sarvebhyo, and all three commentators explain śarva as a vocative (‘O Śarva’) and sarvataḥ (‘everywhere’). The base appears to have the two words in each other’s places.

translation.literal: To the not-terrible, and to the terrible, to the more-terrible-than-terrible, to all, O Śarva, to the Śarva [forms] — homage be to your forms of Rudra.
translation.readable: To your gentle forms and your terrible forms, and to those more terrible still — to all your forms of Rudra, O Śarva, everywhere, be homage.

anvaya: [हे] सर्व, ते अघोरेभ्यः अथ घोरेभ्यः घोरघोरतरेभ्यः सर्वेभ्यः रुद्ररूपेभ्यः शर्वेभ्यः नमः अस्तु ।
syntax: A single sentence: the subject namaḥ with the imperative astu, and a string of datives naming whom the homage is for — the forms (rūpebhyaḥ) of Rudra, described as not-terrible, terrible and more terrible, and as all. The vocative (sarva as printed; śarva in the commentators’ texts) addresses the god himself; te (‘your’) makes the forms his.

ambiguities.note: As printed the text addresses ‘O all’ and names ‘the Śarvas’. The commentators all read ‘O Śarva … to all’: Sāyaṇa «हे शर्व परमेश्वर» and «सर्वेभ्यो रुद्ररूपेभ्यः»; Bhāskara «हे शर्व! ते त्वदीयेभ्यो ऽंशेभ्यः».
The anonymous commentator and Sāyaṇa match the three adjectives to the three guṇas: gentle as sattva, fierce as rajas, most terrible as tamas. The text gives the three degrees, not the guṇas.

metre.name: irregular
metre.note: Close to an anuṣṭubh: the lines count 15 and 18 syllables (the first pāda of each has a syllable fewer or more than eight). Sāyaṇa’s order (sarvataḥ śarva sarvebhyo) has the same count.

beginner: This is the third of the five ‘brahma’ mantras to the faces of Śiva. It names the face called Aghora, ‘not terrible’, and bows to every form the god takes: the gentle ones, the terrible ones, and those more terrible still. The old commentators say these are the three kinds of form: calm, fierce and darkest, matching the three qualities that Indian philosophy finds in all things. The point is that all of them are his, and all receive the same homage. The commentators also note that the words for ‘all’ and ‘Śarva’ (a name of Śiva) have changed places in the text as printed here; their own texts read ‘O Śarva, to all your forms’. The prayer does not ask for anything; it acknowledges that the frightening is as much the god’s as the gentle.
analogy: Like greeting a mountain in fair weather and in storm with the same respect: it is one mountain.

commentary.label: direct
commentary.text: It offers homage to the forms of Rudra, gentle, terrible and more terrible, to all of them, addressing the god.

commentary.q: Which face is this, and what are the three kinds of form?
commentary.label: traditional
commentary.text: The anonymous commentator: the mantra of the southern face, «दक्षिणवक्त्रप्रतिपादकं मन्त्रमाह». Of its forms, some are gentle, «विग्रहा अघोराः सात्विकत्वेन शान्ताः सौम्याः», others fierce, «अन्ये तु घोरा राजसत्वेनोग्राः», and others more terrible still, «अपरे तु तामसत्वेन घोरादपि». Sāyaṇa gives the same account.

commentary.q: To whom is the homage offered, and where?
commentary.label: traditional
commentary.text: Sāyaṇa reads the god addressed as Śarva and the homage as offered everywhere and always: «हे शर्व परमेश्वर ते त्वदीयेभ्यः पूर्वोक्तेभ्यस्त्रिविधेभ्यः सर्वेभ्यो रुद्ररूपेभ्यः», then «सर्वतः सर्वेषु देशेषु सर्वेषु च कालेषु नमोऽस्तु». Bhāskara: the parts of the god, with body, speech and mind: «हे शर्व! ते त्वदीयेभ्यो ऽंशेभ्यः सर्वतः सर्वप्रकारं शिरसा वचसा मनसा च नमोस्तु».

commentary.q: What is meant by the god here?
commentary.label: traditional
commentary.text: Bhāskara: here too brahman is meant, as the totality of the Rudras: «अत्रापि रुद्रसमष्ट्यात्मकं ब्रह्म प्रतिपाद्यम्».

commentary.label: linguistic
commentary.text: The base reads sarvebhyas sarva śarvebhyo; the Tirupati e-text reads sarvataḥ śarva sarvebhyo, which is also Sāyaṇa’s text and the reading every commentator explains. The sources page classes the place ‘verification required’. The hiatus te astu is kept by every witness.

schools.disagreement: No Vedānta-school commentary on this text is in the edition’s sources (Raṅgarāmānuja’s commentary on the Mahānārāyaṇa is not available here). The anonymous commentator and Sāyaṇa read the three kinds of form by the guṇas; Bhāskara reads them as parts of the one brahman as the totality of Rudras.

contemporary.text: The mantra bows equally to the gentle and to the terrible. Much of life asks for that kind of even regard toward what we would rather not meet. This is a modern reflection on the passage, not part of its traditional meaning.

reflect.beginner: Can you respect something you find frightening?
reflect.deeper: Why might a hymn insist that the terrible forms are ‘yours’, the god’s own, rather than another power’s?
reflect.practice: Name one difficult thing in your week without calling it an enemy.

references.text: This is Sāyaṇa’s and Bhāskara’s anuvāka 45 (the third of the pañca-brahma anuvākas).

flags.note: sarvebhyas sarva śarvebhyo (base, Ānandāśrama) against sarvataḥ śarva sarvebhyo (Tirupati, Sāyaṇa’s text, all three commentators); classed ‘verification required’.
The guṇa reading of the three kinds of form is the commentators’; the text has only the three degrees.
